text:
Air Travel Thrust Into Front Lines of War

Governments

caution on flying to

Saudi Arabia after

Houthi airport strike

By BENJAMIN KATZ

Commercial air travel has been dragged into the front lines of escalating conflicts across the globe, with airports, planes and airspace becoming the deliberate target of missile and drone attacks on a scale not seen before.

Since the U.S. and Israel started the Iran war in February, major airports across the Middle East have been repeatedly targeted. Parked aircraft have been hit by missiles or falling debris from interceptor systems, killing crew members and passengers. The threat culminated Saturday in a Houthi missile strike at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300 others.

The strike, the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade, left airlines scrambling to divert scores of aircraft and cancel more than 1,000 other flights. Authorities reported new attacks on the closed airport Sunday, saying a projectile caused a fire in Terminal 4 and led to injuries.

Governments including the U.S., U.K. and Australia are telling citizens to avoid the Riyadh airport following the attack. France, Canada and Germany are warning airlines that flying over all or large parts of Saudi Arabia is no longer safe.

Experts and safety advocates say travelers shouldn't take an airline's decision to fly as a guarantee of a route's safety. "All of this is up to the individual country managing its airspace, and the airline to conduct its own risk assessment," said Matt Borie, chief intelligence officer at aviation security specialist Osprey Flight Solutions. "They're counting on the country to have done the right things to keep the airspace safe," he said.



An image of Riyadh's King Khalid airport from a video posted on social media after Yemen's Houthis attacked it Saturday.

Since late February, Iran has blown up fuel tanks and damaged parked aircraft, runways and air-traffic control infrastructure across major airports in Dubai, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and elsewhere. Israeli strikes have meanwhile hit targets at Beirut Airport, while Saudi Arabia bombed Yemen's San'a Airport in July to prevent a plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing.

The increasing threat to civilian aircraft has prompted rare rebukes from the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations body that governs global air travel, which last month reiterated a call for member states to prevent aviation from being dragged into ongoing hostilities.

The warnings over Saudi Arabian skies, which had been regarded as one of the few safe passages through the Middle East, are pushing airlines to scale back flying in what had become one of only two primary corridors left linking Europe and Asia.

Airlines have repeatedly had to alter flight paths to account for global conflicts, with the rapidly shrinking airspace proving painful at a time when jet fuel is trading at about twice the price it was this time last year.

The shifts began in earnest with the closure of Ukrainian skies in early 2022 and Moscow's subsequent ban on European, U.S. and other carriers using its skies. The closure of a critical corridor over Iraq at the start of the Iran war this year pushed more airlines to fly through Saudi airspace. Increasingly, airlines have been relying on a sliver of airspace passing over Georgia, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan to travel between Europe and Asia.

Virgin Atlantic, for example, has been flying its twice-daily route from Mumbai to London via central Asia since late September. The airline previously routed it frequently through Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

Carriers often are left with no good options. Air India and Turkish Airlines have shifted some routes so that their aircraft fly along the Saudi-Iraq border further away from threats of Houthi attacks. But those flight paths typically pass near Syria's capital, Damascus, which is still regarded as a risky zone.
